\textbf{Source.} Tadelis (2013), \emph{Game Theory: An Introduction}, Exercise 12.9 ``Grab the Dollar'', p.~269 {[}PDF p.~288{]}. Reproduced verbatim. \textbf{Answer in the source:} no (none in the book; Princeton UP's website has about half, not checked).

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Grab the Dollar:} Each of two players has two possible actions: grab the dollar or don't grab the dollar. Player \(i\)'s payoff is 1 if he is the only one to grab the dollar, and his payoff is 0 if he does not. Each player's payoff is \(-1\) if both players grab the dollar.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\alph{enumi}.}
\item
  Find the Nash equilibria of this game of complete information.
\item
  Consider the following perturbation of the game. The payoff structure is the same, with the following addition: When player \(i\) is the only one to grab the dollar his payoff is \(1 + \theta_i\), where \(\theta_i\) is player \(i\)'s type and it is uniformly distributed over \([-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\) with \(\varepsilon < 1\). Each player knows only his own type, and the distribution of types is common knowledge. Find the pure-strategy Bayesian Nash equilibrium of this game of incomplete information.
\item
  Show that when \(\varepsilon\) converges to 0, the pure-strategy Bayesian Nash equilibrium converges to the mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium of the game with complete information.
\end{enumerate}
\end{quote}
